study.title: Karnataka groundwater year book 2022-23: a wet year lifts the state's wells
study.summary: CGWB's 2022-23 year book for Karnataka: ~28% excess rain in 2022 lifted shallow wells state-wide (88% within 10 m before the monsoon, 98% during it), while deep hard-rock pockets near Tumkur and Kolar stayed stressed. 6263 station rows, 8 fluctuation comparisons, 19 map plates, 12 long-record hydrographs.

layers.name: Monitoring network (Plate-I + Table-1)
layers.description: 1413 dug wells + 262 piezometers May/Aug/Nov 2022, growing to 2146 stations in Jan 2023; blue dug well, red piezometer.

layers.name: Drainage basins and geology (Plates II-III)
layers.description: Krishna system 60%, Cauvery 18% of state area; hard crystalline granite-gneiss terrain holding water only in cracks.

layers.name: 2022 rainfall maps (Figs 1-4)
layers.description: Pre-monsoon Excess nearly everywhere; SW monsoon +20% Excess; NE monsoon near-normal; annual +28% Excess. One printed 'Deficit' word quarantined.

layers.name: Depth-to-water maps, shallow aquifer (Plates IV, VI, VIII, X)
layers.description: State within 10 m: May 88%, Aug 98%, Nov 94%, Jan 81%. Deep pockets in Bagalkot, Bidar upland, coast.

layers.name: Piezometric surface maps, deep aquifers (Plates V, VII, IX, XI)
layers.description: Within 10 m: May 45%, Aug/Nov 69%, Jan 58%. Persistent >20-40 m bullseyes near Tumakuru, Kolar fringe, Chamarajanagar tip.

layers.name: Year-on-year fluctuation maps (Plates XII-XV)
layers.description: May/Aug mostly rises vs prior year; Nov/Jan mostly falls. Rises above 4 m in the southern two-thirds.

layers.name: Decadal-mean fluctuation maps (Plates XVI-XIX)
layers.description: May/Aug beat the 10-year mean almost everywhere; Nov split west-down/central-up; Jan below mean at most wells.

layers.name: 12 long-record hydrograph stations (report pp83-85)
layers.description: Decade-plus well records: steady levels with dry-year spikes; Kolar gold-field belt deepest with dramatic 2021-2022 recovery.

layers.name: Bengaluru focus: city and rural wells
layers.description: City-first story: 81/93/80/90 rural+urban station rows per season, district behaviour, and the shallow city hydrograph well.

layers.name: Annexure-I station records, May 2022 (1543 wells)
layers.description: Every May 2022 station row as a reported reference point; GL/Dry/>100 cells preserved as missing, deep outliers confidence-quarantined.

layers.name: Annexure-II station records, Aug 2022 (1623 wells)
layers.description: Every August 2022 station row as a reported reference point; S.No 1-1623 continuous.

layers.name: Annexure-III station records, Nov 2022 (1534 wells)
layers.description: Every November 2022 station row; blank taluk cells and deepest printed levels kept verbatim with caution flags.

layers.name: Annexure-IV station records, Jan 2023 (1563 wells)
layers.description: Every January 2023 station row; Yadgir appears as a district for the first time in the piezometer table.

chart_series.title: Share of shallow wells within 10 m bgl, May 2022 - Jan 2023
chart_series.description: State share of 1312/1335/1406/1558 dug wells with depth to water under 10 m bgl. Lower depth means water nearer the surface.

chart_series.title: Share of deep-well pressure levels within 10 m bgl, May 2022 - Jan 2023
chart_series.description: State share of 191/201/211/243 piezometers with piezometric surface under 10 m bgl; deep levels run much deeper than open wells.

chart_series.title: Median depth to water: state vs Bengaluru, May vs August 2022
chart_series.description: Sample medians, not matched-well rises: station sets differ between seasons. Smaller values mean water nearer the surface.

chart_series.title: 2022 rainfall actual vs normal by season (state)
chart_series.description: Early-2022 showers brought roughly double the normal rain; the main monsoon added a fifth above normal.

chart_series.title: 2022 rainfall departure from normal by season (state)
chart_series.description: Departure classes: Excess at +20% or more, Normal -19% to +19%, Deficit at -20% or worse. All four 2022 periods were Excess or high-Normal.

chart_series.title: Bengaluru shallow-well share within 10 m bgl by season
chart_series.description: Shares computed from printed district counts; city wells deepened faster than rural wells by January.

chart_series.title: Year-on-year well rises vs falls by season (state totals)
chart_series.description: Shares from printed table totals. May and August gained year-on-year; November and January fell as the wet 2022 base year reset comparisons.

chart_series.title: Wells above vs below the 10-year mean by season (state totals)
chart_series.description: Table counts are authoritative where narratives disagree (Aug decadal narrative 80/20 replaced by table 85.4/14.6).

chart_series.title: District rainfall departure extremes, 2022 (% of normal)
chart_series.description: One village got about ten times the rain of another: station extremes 560 mm at Molkarmuru vs 5765 mm at Hebri.

chart_series.title: Bengaluru 2022 rainfall departure from normal (% of normal)
chart_series.description: Bengaluru city and surroundings both had an exceptionally wet 2022 in every season.

chart_series.title: May 2022 depth-to-water band distribution (1312 wells, state)
chart_series.description: Before the monsoon nearly 9 in 10 wells still held water within 10 m of the surface; deep water was confined to Bagalkot/Bijapur pockets.

chart_series.title: Bengaluru year-on-year rise share by season (computed from printed counts)
chart_series.description: Deterministic derivation: rise wells divided by analysed wells per printed district row. Bengaluru swung from strong first-half rises to January falls.

chart_series.title: November 2022 depth-to-water band distribution (1406 wells, state)
chart_series.description: Post-monsoon shape behind the 94%-within-10 m headline: most wells sat at 2-5 m, with a thin 5% tail at 10-20 m and under 1% beyond 20 m. Source band shares printed as 32/38/24/5/0.9/0.1%.

chart_series.title: May 2022 deep-aquifer (piezometric) depth bands (191 piezometers)
chart_series.description: Synthesis label: the deep system in plain words. Unlike shallow dug wells (88% within 10 m), under half of piezometers were within 10 m before the monsoon; 36% sat at 10-20 m, 16% at 20-40 m and about 3% beyond 40 m (Tumkur, Kolar, Chamarajanagar). Aggregated 0-10 m band is used because the source does not split it here.

chart_series.title: Where Karnataka's rain drains: river-system share of state area
chart_series.description: Context view (not a measurement of groundwater): about 3 of every 5 hectares drain to the Krishna system. West-flowing share (13%) is a deterministic remainder (100 minus printed shares) and is labelled derived, never a printed measurement.

chart_series.title: Seasonal split of annual rain: normal year vs wet 2022
chart_series.description: Why 2022 felt unusual before the monsoon even arrived: pre-monsoon showers supplied 16% of the year's rain against a normal 10%, while the main SW monsoon share dipped from 74% to 69%.

chart_series.title: Monitoring network growth: May-Nov 2022 vs January 2023
chart_series.description: The network itself changed mid-year: piezometers/tube wells tripled from 262 to 780 by January 2023 while dug wells eased from 1413 to 1366. Season comparisons therefore use different station sets.

chart_series.title: Commonest year-on-year move per season (share of compared wells)
chart_series.y_label: Share of wells in commonest band
chart_series.description: Most wells move only a little: the single commonest band is always 0-2 m. August share (49.1%) is a deterministic derivation (598 of 1218 wells) from printed counts; all other shares are printed.

chart_series.title: Long-record wells: typical depth range per hydrograph station (figure-derived, approximate)
chart_series.description: Approximate typical ranges read from printed hydrograph axes/summaries, not digitised measurements. The point is the contrast: coastal Udupi breathes at 5-15 m while the Kolar gold-field record lived at 15-35 m. Use as a visual callout, not as data.

chart_series.title: Bengaluru typical (median) depth to water across all four seasons
chart_series.description: Bengaluru scope sample medians (Rural+Urban rows pooled as extracted): 3.99 m in May, 2.29 m in August, 2.22 m in November, then 4.5 m by January. Station sets differ by season, so read this as typical depth per snapshot, not one well tracked over time. Smaller is nearer the surface.

chart_series.title: Districts with the shallowest wells: share within 2 m of the surface
chart_series.description: Where water sat almost at the surface. In May the shallow leaders were Mandya, Tumkur and Davanagere; by August recharge pushed Chitradurga to 96% within 2 m. Minority deep districts (Bidar, Kodagu) are carried in the district resource and layer narrative, not hidden by this leaders view.

figure_panels.title: Sugur (140030075394001): flat with a one-time spike
figure_panels.summary: Flat 0-4 m record interrupted by a single ~20 m deep reading from Nov 2016 to May 2017, then flat again — a stress spike, not a trend.

figure_panels.title: Shimoga (135000075360001): flashy monsoon swings
figure_panels.summary: Levels bounce between 2 and 7 m with the seasons and ease after 2012 — a healthy, rain-responsive well.

figure_panels.title: Manvi2 (160000077020001): deepened, then recovered
figure_panels.summary: Water sank toward 10-11 m around 2015-2016, then climbed back — recovery after a dry spell.

figure_panels.title: Mysore (121800076383001): steady with an old spike
figure_panels.summary: Mostly 8-11 m with a >20 m spike back in 2012; earliest ticks are clipped and uncertain.

figure_panels.title: Krishnarajapet (12400007629001): a stepped plateau
figure_panels.summary: Levels stepped down to about 14 m and sat there through 2013-2017 — like a staircase, not a slide.

figure_panels.title: Yelburga (153810076011001): noisy 4-13 m
figure_panels.summary: Jumpy 4-13 m record with no clear direction — the aquifer breathes hard each year.

figure_panels.title: KGF (125845078154201): the deepest record
figure_panels.summary: The hardest-worked well in the book: 15-35 m, peaking 2014-2015 and 2019-2020, recovering to ~10-16 m by 2021-2022.

figure_panels.title: Kolar (130730078073001): deep, then a dramatic recovery
figure_panels.summary: Ran 15-45 m for years, then recovered steeply below 10 m in 2021-2022 — the wet year's signature.

figure_panels.title: Virajpet1 (121200075480001): twin stress peaks
figure_panels.summary: Shallow 4-13 m with twin ~17 m peaks in 2016-2017 — stress years written into the curve.

figure_panels.title: Udupi (132000074450001): textbook coastal sawtooth
figure_panels.summary: Clean 5-15 m seasonal sawtooth — the coast's rain in, rain out rhythm.

figure_panels.title: Bengaluru (125505077350501): the city well
figure_panels.summary: Bengaluru's own long record: shallow 2-6 m with ~8 m spikes in 2014 and 2016 — the study-scope city anchor.

figure_panels.title: Belgaum1 (155200074300001): steady seasonal
figure_panels.summary: Regular 2-8 m seasonal swings — a well-behaved northern record.

figure_panels.title: Rainfall map plates Figs 1-4: a wet year in four snapshots
figure_panels.summary: Choropleth legends transcribed from the printed maps: pre-monsoon Excess almost everywhere (Bidar the lone Normal), SW monsoon +20% Excess, NE monsoon near-normal with a single Udupi Deficit, annual +28% Excess. One printed closing word 'Deficit' for the annual state total conflicts with its own table and is quarantined, not mapped.

figure_panels.title: Depth-to-water map plates IV, VI, VIII, X (shallow aquifer)
figure_panels.summary: Five-class legends (<2, 2-5, 5-10, 10-20, >20 m bgl; Nov/Jan base class printed 0-2). Blue <2 m spreads state-wide by August, then retreats into a Raichur-Ballari-Bengaluru-Mandya belt by January. Legends are the renderable evidence; no district boundaries are invented.

figure_panels.title: Piezometric map plates V, VII, IX, XI (deep aquifers)
figure_panels.summary: Six-class legends (<2 to >40 m bgl). Shallow <2 m blocks in the north-east contrast with persistent 20-40 m and >40 m bullseyes near Bengaluru, Tumakuru and the Kolar fringe in every season - the deep stress signal of the book.

figure_panels.title: Fluctuation map plates XII-XIX: year-on-year and decadal change
figure_panels.summary: Rise (blue) vs fall (pink/red) in 0-2, 2-4 and >4 m bands. Annual plates flip from rise-dominated (May/Aug) to fall-dominated (Nov/Jan); decadal plates stay rise-dominated in May/Aug. Plate-XVIII legend unit is misprinted 'Fluctuation(ml)' in the source and is noted, not corrected silently.

figure_panels.title: Basemap plates I-III: stations, drainage and geology
figure_panels.summary: Plate-I station dots (blue dug well, red piezometer), Plate-II drainage basins (Krishna largest), Plate-III geology (granite-gneiss and schist terrain with basalt in the north). These plates orient every other view; they carry no invented boundaries.

objects.reason: Back-cover Hindi slogan and imprint; report identity already captured; explicitly deferred with value reason in coverage audit.
Per-point hydrograph values not digitised (dense seasonal ticks); 12 panels retained as figure_panels with metadata and trends.

dispositions.reason: Single sentence calls the wet year 'Deficit' against its own +28% numbers; sentence quarantined, table values used.
Summary '-5% Bidar' vs Table-3 '+5%'; table value used, summary figure flagged.
August decadal narrative 80/20 replaced by table counts 85.4/14.6 wherever rendered.
Three-way August annual conflict; table counts (874/1218) authoritative.
Tumkur 97.5/>100 m and Kolar 64.6 m readings are source-printed deep-well values; features carry low confidence, rows retained.
Blank taluks kept missing; deepest printed levels (Nov 122 m, Jan 128 m Tumkur SIRA) kept verbatim with low confidence.

limitations: No coordinates in source: 6263 station features are reported reference points (taluk/village names), usable for filtering and tables, not precise map pins.
No logged intervals in source: vertical profiles and intervals are empty by design; total depths support no synthetic geology.
Hydrograph per-point values not digitised; panels carry metadata and trends only.
Four merged district pairs reported as 27 units though the state has 31 districts (GEMS/WIMS software).
Table-19 prints only 23 district rows (Bagalkot, Shimoga, Uttara Kannada absent); pre-monsoon Bidar and NE counts carry table-vs-narrative flags.

semantic_presentation.focus: Bengaluru city within a wet state year
semantic_presentation.map_note: Choropleth plate legends (I-XIX) plus unlocated station coverage; no invented boundaries or fallback geography.
semantic_presentation.default_story: Start in Bengaluru (hero layer), widen to the shallow-aquifer depth maps and the wet-2022 rainfall maps, then open deep-aquifer, fluctuation and hydrograph layers on demand. Station annexes stay archived behind filters so 6263 rows never bury the 16 curated stories.
semantic_presentation.chart_story: Headline shares first (CS-PHREATIC-SHALLOW, CS-PIEZO-SHALLOW), distributions second (CS-MAY/NOV-BANDS, CS-MAY-PIEZO-BANDS), Bengaluru and fluctuation comparisons third, context shares (drainage, season split, network growth) last. Figure-derived hydrograph ranges are labelled approximate.

study.title: Karnataka groundwater year book 2022-23: a wet year lifts the state's wells
study.summary: CGWB's 2022-23 year book for Karnataka: ~28% excess rain in 2022 lifted shallow wells state-wide (88% within 10 m before the monsoon, 98% during it), while deep hard-rock pockets near Tumkur and Kolar stayed stressed. 6263 station rows, 8 fluctuation comparisons, 19 map plates, 12 long-record hydrographs.

target_insights.analysis: This book is the Central Ground Water Board’s yearly health check of Karnataka’s underground water for 2022–23, covering the whole state (about 192,000 sq km, 31 districts). About 1,675 wells were measured three times in 2022, growing to about 2,150 monitoring points by January 2023. The headline finding: 2022 was a wet year, with roughly 28% more rain than normal, and shallow wells across the state sat high — about 94% held water within 10 metres of the surface after the monsoon. The stressed exception is deep underground near Tumkur and Kolar, where pipe sensors read water more than 100 metres down in hard rock under heavy pumping. Bengaluru’s city and rural wells shared fully in the wet year.

This layer shows how the watch itself is organised. The state runs about 1,413 shallow open wells plus 262 deeper pipe sensors (piezometers), measured on fixed dates four times a year, with extra monthly checks at selected Bengaluru city wells. Shallow open wells tap the top water layer, usually within 20 metres; the deeper pipes can read a different, deeper level at the same place. Only the shallow-well readings feed the book’s water-level maps. Because of the database software, four pairs of neighbouring districts are reported merged, so the analysis uses 27 reporting units instead of 31 districts.

This layer sets the stage: where rain drains and what rock it sinks into. Six of every ten drops that stay in the state drain to the Krishna river system; the Cauvery takes about two in ten, and the rest goes to smaller east-flowing rivers plus short west-flowing coastal streams. Most of Karnataka sits on ancient, hard granite-like rock with almost no sponge-like pore space — groundwater lives only where the rock is cracked, weathered, or dissolved, with small volcanic and limestone patches as exceptions. That is why water levels can differ sharply over short distances.

This layer tells the rainfall story behind everything else. A district counts as excess at 120% or more of its usual rain, normal near the average, and deficit at 80% or below. Early-2022 showers brought roughly double the usual rain (state +98%, nearly every district in excess); the main June–September monsoon added about a fifth above normal; the retreating monsoon was near normal overall (+17%); and the year closed about 28% above normal with 24 of 31 districts in excess. One printed sentence calling the wet year a deficit contradicts its own table and is ignored; the table numbers are used.

Depth to water means how far down you must go from the ground surface to reach water, in metres below ground level (m bgl) — a smaller number means a fuller well. This layer tracks the shallow aquifer through the year: 88% of wells sat within 10 metres before the monsoon (May), 98% during it (August), 94% after it (November), and 81% by the following January as levels eased down. The deepest shallow wells are isolated pockets in the north, chiefly Bagalkot, which held the state maximum in three of the four seasons.

A piezometer is a narrow pipe that reads the pressure level of a deeper, often confined water layer — not the open shallow well. This layer shows those deeper levels are far more stressed: only 45% sat within 10 metres before the monsoon, rising to 69% during and after it, then falling to 58% by January. The extremes are dramatic: Tumkur’s deep test well read 97.5 metres down in May and 128 metres by January, and Kolar’s gold-field wells read beyond 70 metres. These bullseyes persist in every season, marking hard-rock zones under heavy draft.

Fluctuation here means this year’s level minus last year’s at the same well and season — a rise means the water table stood higher (a smaller depth number). Compared with the previous year, May and August 2022 rose at most wells (about 89% and 72%), with rises above 4 metres across the southern two-thirds. November and January flipped: most wells fell, and by January only about 18% still stood higher than the year before. In short, the wet monsoon filled the wells, then the dry months drew them down again.

This layer compares 2022 against each well’s own 10-year average for that season — a tougher test than last year alone. May and August 2022 beat their decade mean at nearly 9 in 10 wells (about 88% and 85%), confirming an unusually full monsoon. November was mixed, with the west down and central districts up. January was the only season to finish below its decade mean at most wells (only about 45% above it), showing the dry-season drawdown outpacing even a wet year’s recharge.

A hydrograph is a decade-plus line chart of one well’s level over time, like a patient’s long health record. This layer anchors 12 such records: most are steady or gently seasonal, with sharp one-time dips after dry years. The standouts are the Kolar gold-field belt wells — the deepest records in the set at 15–45 metres — which staged a steep recovery back below 10 metres in 2021–22 after the wet years. The city well in Bengaluru itself stays shallow (2–6 metres) with only brief spikes.

This is the city-first story. Bengaluru’s urban wells and the surrounding rural wells (reported together with today’s Ramanagara-area taluks) both enjoyed excess rain in all four seasons — the city finished the year about 72% above normal, the rural belt about 88% above. Shallow medians ran 2–4 metres in the city and rural May/August rounds, deepening only modestly by January (no urban or rural well passed 20 metres). Year-on-year, both districts swung from strong May/August rises to January falls, and against the 10-year mean August 2022 rose at every rural well measured.

This is the raw May 2022 station archive: one row per monitored well (1,543 rows) with district, taluk, village or station name, aquifer class, and that month’s depth to water in metres. Blank, dry (GL) and over-100-metre cells are kept as missing, never as zero. Use it to filter and count wells; the state-wide pattern it supports is that nearly 9 in 10 wells stood within 10 metres before the monsoon.

This is the raw August 2022 station archive: one row per monitored well (1,623 rows) with the same district-to-level layout as May plus a serial column. It captures the monsoon peak, when all but about 2% of wells stood within 10 metres of the surface. Missing and dry cells are preserved as missing throughout.

This is the raw November 2022 station archive: one row per monitored well (1,534 rows) catching the post-monsoon high, when 94% of wells stood within 10 metres. One printed state total (a single well beyond 40 metres) has no matching district row and the narrative assigns it to Kolar; the archive keeps the district rows as printed.

This is the raw January 2023 station archive: one row per monitored well (1,563 rows) catching the dry-season drawdown, when only about 81% of wells still stood within 10 metres and roughly 18% sat at 10–20 metres. Yadgir appears as a district in the piezometer table for the first time this season.

Bangalore Rural here is the book’s grouping, which still includes the Channapatna, Kanakapura, Magadi and Ramanagara taluks of today’s Ramanagara district. Its shallow wells ran full all year: the typical (median) depth was about 4 metres in May, improving to about 2.3 metres in August when two-thirds of wells sat within 2 metres of the surface, and no well passed 14 metres even in January. Its deeper pipe sensors ranged far wider (roughly 0.6–30 metres), showing the deep layer under more pressure than the shallow one.

These are Bengaluru city’s own monitored wells: 19 in May, growing to 35 by January. Before the monsoon, depths spanned nearly the surface (0.05 metres) to about 13 metres; during the monsoon every city well stood within 10 metres with three-fifths within 2 metres. After the monsoon a few city wells deepened — five sat at 10–20 metres and two beyond 20 metres in November — but by January none passed 20 metres. The city’s long-record well on page 85 confirms this picture, holding 2–6 metres across the decade with only brief spikes.

This marks the state’s most stressed deep zone. Near Sira in Tumkur district, a deep test well read water 97.5 metres down in May 2022 and 128 metres down by January 2023 — deeper than a 40-storey building is tall. These are pressure levels in deep, fractured hard rock that refills slowly while pumping runs heavy, so they stay deep even in a wet year when shallow wells nearby are full. Treat this as a deep-aquifer warning light, not as the level of ordinary open wells.

This marks the Kolar gold-field belt, the state’s second stressed deep zone. Kolar’s deep wells read down to about 73 metres in May and 65 metres in August — again, deep hard-rock pressure levels, not village open wells. The hopeful counterpoint sits in the decade-long records: Kolar’s long-record wells climbed from 15–45 metres back below 10 metres in 2021–22, the steepest recovery in the book, showing this rock can rebound when rains are generous.

This well’s decade-long record is almost flat, hovering within 0–4 metres of the surface — until a single dramatic dip to about 20 metres between late 2016 and mid-2017, after which it returned to normal. Think of it as a patient with one bad fever episode and an otherwise clean bill of health.

This well swings up and down with the rains between about 2 and 7 metres — a flashy, rain-responsive record — and the swings have gentled since about 2012. It is a good example of a healthy shallow well that breathes with the monsoon.

This well deepened noticeably to about 10–11 metres in the dry years of 2015–16, then climbed back as rains returned. It shows how a run of poor monsoons can push a well down and how recovery follows when the rains come back.

This well normally sits at 8–11 metres, but its record carries one sharp dip beyond 20 metres back in 2012. Since then it has held its normal band — a stable well with one historical stress mark worth knowing about.

This well stepped down to a deeper plateau of about 14 metres during 2013–17 and stayed there for years, like water finding a new, lower shelf. Its flat steps show a well that adjusted to a drier spell rather than swinging wildly.
This well’s record is noisy, bouncing anywhere from 4 to 13 metres with no smooth pattern. The scatter itself is the message: at this spot, local pumping and fractures matter as much as the season.

This is the deepest long record in the book: the Kolar Gold Fields well swung between 15 and 35 metres for years, peaking around 2014–15 and 2019–20. By 2021–22 it had recovered to about 10–16 metres — still deep, but the strongest healing trend among the deep wells.

This Kolar town well ran the deepest of all, between 15 and 45 metres, then staged a steep climb back below 10 metres in 2021–22. Paired with the KGF well, it tells the book’s most hopeful deep-aquifer story: even severely drawn-down hard rock can rebound after generous rains.

This Coorg-hills well is normally shallow (4–13 metres) but shows twin sharp dips to about 17 metres in 2016–17. Two bad years in a row left a visible double mark, then the record recovered — a signature of back-to-back weak monsoons.

This coastal well is the textbook example of a seasonal sawtooth: levels rise and fall between 5 and 15 metres every single year, as regular as breathing. If you want to show a beginner what monsoon recharge looks like, show this well.

This is the study-scope city well for Bengaluru: shallow at 2–6 metres across the decade, with brief dips to about 8 metres in 2014 and 2016. It confirms that the city’s shallow layer has held up, even as individual neighbourhood wells vary.
This well traces a steady seasonal sawtooth between 2 and 8 metres — up with the monsoon, down in the dry months, year after year. It is the picture of a well in balance with its rains.

Karnataka’s wettest and driest ground in 2022 sat about 500 km apart. Coastal Udupi received 4,672 mm — over 4.5 metres of rain, more than six times Koppal’s 744 mm in the dry interior. The coast catches the monsoon full-force off the Arabian Sea while the interior sits in the Western Ghats’ rain shadow. This single contrast explains much of the state’s water-level geography.

Bagalkot district held the state’s deepest shallow-well readings in three of the four seasons: 29.5 metres in May, 24.7 in August, and 27.3 in November. Crucially, these are isolated pockets — only about 1% of the state’s wells sat beyond 20 metres — not a district-wide crisis. They mark spots where local rock and pumping keep a few wells deep even while neighbours fill.

limitations: All 6281 features are unlocated (source prints no coordinates); analyses describe district/station evidence without invented pins.
Four district pairs reported merged (27 units); Bangalore Rural includes present-day Ramanagara taluks.

report.display_title: Karnataka’s groundwater in a wet year: the 2022-23 year book
report.brief_description: CGWB’s 2022-23 year book for Karnataka: ~28% excess rain lifted shallow wells state-wide while deep hard-rock pockets near Tumkur and Kolar stayed stressed.

blocks.headline: A wet year lifted the state’s shallow wells; deep hard-rock pockets stayed stressed
blocks.content: Think of this book as an annual health check of Karnataka’s underground water. About 1,675 open wells and pipe sensors — growing to roughly 2,150 points by January 2023 — were measured four times. The state received 1,474 mm of rain against a 1,153 mm normal, so shallow wells sat high all year: 88% within 10 metres of the surface before the monsoon, 98% during it, 94% after it, easing to 81% by January. Far below, deep pipe sensors near Tumkur and Kolar read beyond 100 metres in hard rock under heavy pumping — a separate deep-aquifer stress story. Bengaluru city and its rural belt shared fully in the wet year.

blocks.headline: Rain came early, stayed through the monsoon, and left the year 28% above normal
blocks.content: Rainfall class is simple: a district is in excess at 120% or more of its usual rain, normal near the average, deficit at 80% or below. January–May showers delivered about double the norm (state +98%, nearly every district excess). The June–September monsoon added a fifth above normal (+20%, 21 districts excess). The October–December retreat was near normal (+17%; coastal Udupi the lone deficit). The year closed at +28% with 24 of 31 districts excess. In 2022 the early showers contributed an unusually big slice (16%) of the annual total. Bengaluru was excess in every season: the city ended ~72% above normal, the rural belt ~88% above.

metrics.label: Wettest vs driest district
metrics.explanation: Coast catches the monsoon; the interior sits in the rain shadow

blocks.headline: Shallow wells filled with the monsoon and eased down by January
blocks.content: Depth to water is the distance from the ground surface down to water — a smaller number means a fuller well. Before the monsoon, nearly 9 in 10 wells stood within 10 metres (shallowest: 0.04 m in Udupi; deepest: 29.5 m in Bagalkot). During the monsoon almost every well in the state filled to within 10 metres (98%). After the monsoon levels stayed high (94%). By January the dry-season pull showed: 4 in 5 wells still within 10 metres, 18% at 10–20 metres, and only isolated pockets beyond 20 metres. Bagalkot held the deepest shallow reading in three seasons, but such pockets are ~1% of wells, not a statewide condition.

blocks.headline: Deep aquifers tell a harder story beneath Tumkur and Kolar
blocks.content: A piezometer is a narrow pipe reading the pressure level of a deeper, often confined layer — a different number from the open well beside it. Only 45% of deep readings sat within 10 metres before the monsoon, rising to 69% during and after it, then 58% by January. The extremes persist every season: Tumkur’s deep test well (97.5 m in May, 128 m by January) and Kolar’s gold-field wells (beyond 70 m). These sit in fractured hard rock that refills slowly while pumping runs heavy. The book’s conclusion keeps the two stories separate: shallow maps use only open-well data.

blocks.headline: Versus last year and the decade: a full monsoon, then a dry-season pullback
blocks.content: Year-on-year, May 2022 stood higher than May 2021 at about 89% of compared wells (most commonly by 0–2 m), and August at about 72%. November flipped to mostly falls and January to only ~18% rises. Against each well’s own 10-year seasonal average, May and August beat the decade mean at nearly 9 in 10 wells — an unusually full monsoon — while January was the lone season to finish below its decade mean at most wells (only ~45% above). The arc is consistent: generous recharge, then normal dry-season withdrawal.

metrics.label: August vs 10-year mean
metrics.display_value: 85.4% of wells above their decade mean

blocks.headline: Bengaluru: a wet year on every measure, shallow wells included
blocks.content: The city’s 19–35 monitored wells and the rural belt’s 33–56 wells (reported with today’s Ramanagara-area taluks) both finished every season in excess. City medians ran about 2–4 metres; in August every city well stood within 10 metres and three-fifths within 2 metres. November brought a few deeper city readings (five at 10–20 m, two beyond 20 m), but January closed with none beyond 20 m. Year-on-year both districts swung from strong May/August rises to January falls, and August beat the decade mean at every rural well measured. The city’s decade-long well confirms the shallow layer’s resilience at 2–6 metres.

blocks.headline: Twelve decade-long wells: mostly steady, with Kolar’s dramatic recovery
blocks.content: Twelve wells carry line charts stretching back a decade or more. Most are calm: the coastal Udupi well ticks up and down 5–15 metres every year like clockwork, and Belgaum traces a steady 2–8 metre sawtooth. Dry years left scars — single deep dips at Sugur and Mysore, twin 2016–17 dips at Virajpet, a mid-decade shelf at Krishnarajapet. The deepest pair, KGF (15–35 m) and Kolar town (15–45 m), both climbed steeply back below 10 metres in 2021–22 — the book’s strongest evidence that even badly drawn-down hard rock can rebound.

metrics.display_value: Kolar town: 15-45 m back below 10 m (2021-22)

blocks.headline: How to read this book without going wrong
blocks.content: Wells were read on fixed dates: the 1st–10th for January and November, the 20th–31st for May and August, with extra monthly reads at selected city wells. Only shallow open-well data feed the level maps; pipe-sensor data describe deeper layers. Depths are in metres below ground level. The analysis merges four district pairs (27 reporting units), and the station archives carry village names without coordinates — so wells support filtering and tables, not precise map pins. Two printed slips are quarantined: a deficit label on an excess-rain paragraph and a mismatched November >40 m total; table rows are used in both cases.

limitations: No coordinates in source: 6263 station features are reported reference points (taluk/village names), usable for filtering and tables, not precise map pins.
No logged intervals in source: vertical profiles and intervals are empty by design; total depths support no synthetic geology.
Hydrograph per-point values not digitised; panels carry metadata and trends only.
Four merged district pairs reported as 27 units though the state has 31 districts (GEMS/WIMS software).
Table-19 prints only 23 district rows (Bagalkot, Shimoga, Uttara Kannada absent); pre-monsoon Bidar and NE counts carry table-vs-narrative flags.
